lesson_title: Same Air, a Third of the Breath
hook_text: The air on top of Everest has the same 21 per cent oxygen as the beach. So why can't climbers breathe?
clip_script: Air is a mixture: about 78 per cent nitrogen, 21 per cent oxygen, almost 1 per cent argon, and a tiny 0,04 per cent carbon dioxide. That mix stays the same as you climb. What changes is how much air there is. Gravity pulls the air down, so the air at the bottom is squashed by all the air above it. Every 5,5 kilometres up, the air gets about half as thick. On top of Everest, each breath holds only about a third of the air you get at sea level. Even in Johannesburg the air is thinner, so water boils at about 94 degrees, chip packets puff up and athletes who train there get a boost at the coast.
visual_style: A tower of 100 coloured balloons sorting into gases; a column of air particles packed tight at the bottom and spread out at the top; a chip packet swelling on a mountain pass.
pacing: Puzzle open, quick balloon breakdown, a slow climb up the air column, a rapid-fire everyday close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and find out where the air actually ends.
